newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Critics dismiss challenge to Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Critics dismiss challenge to Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: Critics have dismissed as a gimmick a proposal by a Swiss right-wing politician who says backers of a humanitarian foundation for victims of the Holocaust and other abuses must pay for it out of own pockets.

Christoph Blocher, who according to a fierce government critic utters in public what cabinet ministers think in private, challenged leading government backers of the planned foundation on Saturday to put their money where their mouth is.
"The concept of this solidarity (foundation) has become an empty one," the populist member of the right-wing Swiss People's Party, told a public meeting in Berne.
Blocher claims the planned seven billion Swiss franc foundation, revealed in March, implies guilt when the Swiss have nothing to be guilty about.

The plan envisages selling part of central bank gold reserves to finance the foundation. Swiss voters must approve the plan in a referendum next year shaping up as a watershed in Swiss foreign and domestic policy.
Blocher's critics dismissed his challenge as a trick, Swiss media reported on Sunday.

"Blocher says what the cabinet is not allowed to say," said Jean Ziegler, a Socialist member of parliament and a critic of the way the government and banks have handled Jewish charges that Switzerland profitted blatantly from World War Two.
"Blocher wants to put up a concrete wall between us and our past," he told German-language newspaper Zonntags Blick.
Blocher's isolationist arguments helped persuade Swiss voters in 1992 to reject closer ties with the European Union.
Opinion polls show public support is already dwindling for the foundation.

Observers say that if Blocher manages to rally enough support to persuade voters to overturn the plan, it would be a real setback for Switzerland, facing charges that its netrality in the middle of a warring Europe was little more than cooperation with the Nazis under a different name.

Blocher called on the leading rich of Switzerland, backers of the plan including the head of the central bank as well as other prominent Swiss figures to donate the equivalent of an annual salary to the foundation.

He said he would follow suit if others put up the money. "My million is ready," he told the Berne meeting held to discuss a scathing U.S. government report in May that alleged the Swiss were bankers to the Nazis.
The report, compiled by U.S. Under-secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, has outraged many Swiss and radicalised the opposition to the humanitarian foundation plan.

"Blocher's suggestion is just whipping up a storm in a teacup," said Peter Arbenz, member of the board of the International Committee of the Red Cross and among people named by Blocher as a potential contributor to the foundation.
"If he is really concerned about giving out a signal of solidarity, then he should donate his million to the foundation for humanity and justice," he told Zonntags Blick.

Swiss businesses have also launched a 265 million Swiss franc (184 million) memorial fund amid boycott threats from Jewish groups, who accuse banks of hoarding the dormant wealth that Jews murdered by Hitler had placed in Switzerland.
Payments from the fund are yet to begin. ( = 1.44 Swiss Francs)
